title: Construction ban in NCR from Nov 5, WFH for 50% in Noida, Gurugram, too
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Nikhil Ghanekar)
syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution and degradation · GS2 › Statutory bodies (CAQM); Health · GS1 › Urbanisation, its problems and remedies
summary: Citing historically peak pollution in November, CAQM ordered a 15-day ban on dust-generating construction across NCR from November 5 and up to 50% work from home.
ideas: From reaction to anticipation: CAQM acted before pollution peaked, citing a recurring pattern of 'Severe' AQI in early to mid-November (2018-2025) and the region's 'seasonal vulnerability'.
GS3 · Pollution control
Pollution control must be anticipatory, acting on known seasonal patterns before air turns severe.
Many sources, one airshed: dust, vehicles, open burning, industry and stubble burning add up, while low winds and a shallow boundary layer trap pollutants.
GS3 · Pollution / GS1 · Climate
Delhi's winter smog combines local emissions with meteorology that traps them.
Graded restrictions with exemptions: essential projects (Railways, Metro, airports, hospitals, water and sanitation, defence) are exempt; highways, flyovers, power lines and pipelines are not.
GS3 · Infrastructure vs environment
Pollution curbs must balance essential services against emissions.
Layers of action: CAQM's ban adds to Delhi's 10-point Winter Action Plan (Nov 1 to Feb 28), which denies fuel to vehicles without valid PUC certificates and bars non-BS-VI outside vehicles.
GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Air quality needs a regional body (CAQM) and city plans working together.
Technology for enforcement: CAQM's Integrated Command and Control Centre uses live camera feeds to spot violations such as open burning.
GS3 · Technology in governance
Real-time monitoring turns pollution rules into enforceable action.
keywords: Managing air quality across a whole region, not one city
Delhi's smog needs an airshed approach across NCR states, which CAQM is meant to provide.
A shallow mixing layer that traps pollutants near the ground
In winter, a shallow boundary layer and weak winds trap pollutants over the Indo-Gangetic plain.
Acting on forecasts and patterns before a crisis
CAQM's November ban is an example of anticipatory regulation.
Pollutants formed when primary emissions react in air
PM2.5 binds with gases to form secondary pollutants, worsening health risks.
Recurring periods when a region is most exposed
Recognising seasonal vulnerability lets authorities plan curbs in advance.
data: November AQI data show a recurring early-to-mid-November peak in 'Severe' and 'Severe+' categories
Eight years of AQI data show NCR's pollution peaks every early November (CAQM).
examples: CAQM's 15-day construction ban
November 5-20 curbs on dust-generating demolition and outdoor construction
GS3 · Pollution / GS2 · Statutory bodies
CAQM's pre-emptive November ban shows a statutory body using data to act before a crisis.
Delhi's Winter Action Plan
No fuel without a valid PUC; non-BS-VI outside vehicles barred
GS2 · Governance / GS3 · Pollution
Delhi's 'no PUC, no fuel' rule links enforcement to a routine point of contact.
Work from home as pollution policy
Up to 50% of staff in Delhi and five NCR districts
GS4
GS3 · Pollution / GS4 · Shared responsibility
Work from home during smog shows citizens and employers sharing responsibility for clean air.
pyqs: Why Delhi's air pollution is worse than Mumbai's or Kolkata's: geography and meteorology.
WHO's revised Air Quality Guidelines and changes needed in NCAP.
Photochemical smog: formation, effects and mitigation.

trend.t: Air pollution entered through geography: why Delhi is worse than other megacities (GS1, 2015). GS3 then tested standards (WHO guidelines and NCAP, 2021) and the science of smog (2022).
trend.watch: Air pollution is asked roughly every few years and swings between science, standards and Delhi's geography. Prepare the causes, the institutions (CAQM, NCAP) and the science together.
focus: Meteorology of winter smog in the Indo-Gangetic plain
Institutions: CAQM, NCAP, GRAP
Sources: dust, vehicles, stubble, industry
Health and economic costs

potential: "Delhi's air crisis is as much a problem of governance as of geography." Discuss. (15 marks)
Evaluate the role of the Commission for Air Quality Management in tackling pollution in the National Capital Region. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Delhi's air crisis is as much a problem of governance as of geography." Discuss.
parts: Introduction: the November pattern, with facts

answer.t: Citing 'Severe' AQI every early November from 2018 to 2025, CAQM has ordered a 15-day construction ban across NCR from November 5.

pts.t: Delhi sits in the Indo-Gangetic plain, far from sea breezes.
Low winds and a shallow boundary layer limit dispersion.
Paddy harvest in Punjab and Haryana coincides with the peak.
Dry conditions and construction raise PM10 and PM2.5.
PM2.5 reacts with gases to form secondary particles.
Pollution crosses state borders.
Many states and agencies share one airshed.
Rules on PUC, dust and burning are weakly enforced.
pts.ex: Delhi now denies fuel without a valid PUC.

pts.t: Curbs often come after the AQI turns severe.
Stubble alternatives are costly for small farmers.
Old vehicles and polluting fuels persist.
Limited real-time data on violations.
pts.ex: CAQM's new command centre uses live feeds.

pts.t: Act on seasonal forecasts.
Joint targets for NCR states under CAQM.
Ex-situ use and machinery support.
Public transport, EVs and BS-VI enforcement.
Mandatory dust norms and green cover.
Work from home and awareness.

answer.t: Geography sets the stage for Delhi's smog, but governance decides how bad it gets, so anticipatory, regional and enforced action is the answer.

title: After dropping plan for highway, Bihar pushes for tourism project in sanctuary
where: Front page Express special, continued on page 2 (Jay Mazoomdaar)
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation; Environmental impact assessment · GS2 › Statutory bodies (National Board for Wildlife); Judiciary · GS4 › Environmental ethics; Conflict of interest
summary: A Bihar Forest Department society has floated a ₹62.87-crore, 60-year tourism tender with cottages and a helipad inside Bhimbandh Wildlife Sanctuary, despite legal restrictions.
ideas: The guardian as developer: the Bihar Eco Tourism Development Society, under the Forest Department, is promoting commercial construction in a sanctuary that department must protect.
GS4 · Conflict of interest / GS3 · Conservation
When the forest department becomes a developer, the regulator's role and the promoter's role collide.

The law sets clear limits: under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, tourist lodges or hotels in a sanctuary need prior approval of the National Board for Wildlife, and the Supreme Court in 2023 restrained construction in protected areas.
GS2 · Statutory bodies / Judiciary
Commercial tourism in sanctuaries needs NBWL approval and must respect the Supreme Court's 2023 restraint.
Ownership is not a licence: land owned by government departments still lies within notified sanctuary limits, so it gets no exemption from the Act.
GS3 · Protected-area law
Notified sanctuary boundaries, not land titles, decide what can be built.
A pattern, not a one-off: in September the same department inked an MoU to ease forest clearance for a highway widening; flagged for conflict of interest, it was cancelled this month.
GS3 · Development vs conservation
Repeated attempts to fast-track projects inside forests show the pressure of development on protected areas.
Eco-tourism or real estate: 104 cottages, a helipad, banquet halls and an auditorium for weddings are mass tourism, not low-impact eco-tourism; the tender is also unclear on who gets clearances.
GS3 · Eco-tourism / EIA
Eco-tourism must be low-impact and community-based; banquet halls and helipads in a sanctuary are not.
keywords: Statutory body whose prior approval is needed for commercial tourism in protected areas
NBWL approval is the legal gate for commercial construction inside sanctuaries.
A regulator acting for the interests it should restrain
A forest department promoting construction in its own sanctuary is a case of regulatory capture.
The level of use an ecosystem can sustain without degrading
Tourism in sanctuaries must stay within ecological carrying capacity.
Low-impact, community-led tourism versus high-footprint commercial tourism
Helipads and banquet halls turn eco-tourism into mass tourism.
Clearing projects piece by piece to avoid scrutiny
Starting construction where clearances are not needed risks salami slicing of a protected area.
examples: Bhimbandh Wildlife Sanctuary
About 682 sq km in Bihar's Kharagpur Hills; hot springs; leopard, sloth bear, hyena, wolf
GS4
GS3 · Conservation / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Bhimbandh shows how tourism projects can threaten protected areas when the regulator becomes the promoter.
Buxa tiger relocation
A tigress moved from Bihar to Bengal's Buxa Tiger Reserve strayed into Assam (page 9)
GS3 · Conservation
The Buxa tigress straying into Assam shows that reintroduction fails without restored habitat and prey.
pyqs: Biodiversity and the legal framework for conservation.
Tourism and the limits of ecological carrying capacity in Himalayan states.
Environmental NGOs and activists in EIA outcomes for major projects.

trend.t: Conservation questions moved from biodiversity law (2018) and wetlands (2018, 2023) to sanctuaries in rainforest regions (2023) and the role of civil society in EIA (2024). Tourism's ecological limits appeared in GS1 (2015), and GS4 now asks about clearances in sensitive areas (2025).
trend.watch: Questions now test the institutions of conservation (EIA, civil society, clearances), not just facts about species. Prepare the legal process along with the ecology.
focus: Protected-area law: WPA, NBWL, Supreme Court orders
EIA and public participation
Eco-tourism and carrying capacity
Development vs conservation dilemmas

potential: "Eco-tourism in protected areas often becomes a gateway for commercialisation." Critically examine with reference to India's legal safeguards. (15 marks)
Discuss the role of the National Board for Wildlife in balancing development and conservation. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Eco-tourism in protected areas often becomes a gateway for commercialisation." Critically examine with reference to India's legal safeguards.
parts: Introduction: the Bhimbandh tender, with facts

answer.t: Bihar's forest department has floated a ₹62.87-crore, 60-year tender for 104 cottages and a helipad inside Bhimbandh Wildlife Sanctuary, though commercial lodges need NBWL approval.

pts.t: Guides, homestays and crafts give communities a stake in conservation.
Entry fees fund protection.
Visitors build public support for wildlife.
Regular visitors can deter poaching.
Wildlife tourism brands a region.
Tourism income can replace mining or logging.
Helipads, banquet halls and auditoriums exceed carrying capacity.
The forest department's society is the developer.
Starting work where clearances are 'not needed'.
A 60-year lease locks in private use.
Noise, lights and roads fragment habitats.
Private operators capture income, not locals.
No commercial lodges without it.
The 2023 Supreme Court restraint on construction.
Cap visitors and structures.
Eco-development committees share revenue.
Independent regulator from promoter.
Public hearings and disclosure.

answer.t: Eco-tourism can protect sanctuaries only if it stays small, community-led and within the law; otherwise it becomes real estate in a forest.

title: 'The opportunity for India is leveraging AI to reimagine how we use machines'
where: Nation, page 14 (Express Rendezvous with Kris Gopalakrishnan); TRAI draft on AI governance, Economy page 23
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: developments and their effects; Employment · GS2 › Education and skills; Regulatory bodies · GS4 › Ethics of technology
summary: Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan says AI will automate coding and freeze entry-level hiring for now, while TRAI proposes board-level accountability for AI in telecom networks.
ideas: A horizontal technology: like computing, AI affects every sector; its first effect is the 'democratisation of intelligent productivity', starting with software coding, though a human is still needed in the loop.
GS3 · Emerging technology
AI, as a horizontal technology, will reshape every sector, starting with knowledge work like coding.

The entry-level squeeze: IT revenues still grow and there are no mass layoffs, but entry-level hiring is almost zero; graduates without AI skills will struggle, and universities lag three to four years.
GS3 · Employment / GS2 · Education
AI is hitting entry-level jobs first, so curricula must catch up quickly.
India's edge is reskilling at scale: low-cost reskilling keeps margins high, and global capability centres are moving research to India.
GS3 · Industry / Human capital
Reskilling at low cost and global capability centres can turn AI disruption into an Indian advantage.
Products need risk capital: India built services without venture capital; product firms need risk capital and market access, and society needs a bigger appetite for risk.
GS3 · Startups / Investment
India's shift from services to products depends on risk capital and a culture that accepts failure.
Accountability for AI: TRAI's draft asks telecom operators to adopt board-approved AI policies and governance committees and to report AI incidents, staying liable even when AI is outsourced.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies / GS3 · Critical infrastructure
AI governance must keep humans and boards accountable, even when systems are bought from vendors.
keywords: A person checks or approves AI outputs
Keeping a human in the loop preserves accountability in AI-driven decisions.
Multinationals' in-house tech and research hubs
The growth of GCCs shows India moving up from outsourcing to research.
AI performance degrading as data change over time
TRAI flags model drift as a risk when AI runs critical networks.
Inputs designed to fool an AI system
Adversarial attacks on AI can threaten critical infrastructure.
Near-zero entry-level IT hiring is a warning of AI-led jobless growth.
data: Employed by the IT industry, out of a population of 1.4-1.5 billion
IT employs about six million people: a high-income niche, not a mass employer.
examples: TRAI's draft AI framework for telecom
Board-approved AI policies, governance committees, incident reporting
GS4
GS2 · Regulation / GS4 · Accountability
TRAI's draft shows regulators making boards answerable for AI failures.
Binance hack
About $6.3 billion stolen in some 20 minutes via a compromised engineer's laptop (Explained, page 20)
GS3 · Cyber security
The Binance hack shows how one compromised device can expose a whole financial system.
pyqs: Agentic AI: applications, risks and challenges.
Demographic dividend and falling employability: where will jobs come from?
Startups, innovation and employment, and their challenges.
AI as an input for administrative decision-making: an ethical view.
potential: "Artificial Intelligence will shrink entry-level jobs before it creates new ones." Discuss the implications for India's demographic dividend. (15 marks)
Why is board-level accountability necessary for the use of AI in critical infrastructure such as telecom? (10 marks)

title: For affordable cancer care, go beyond price caps
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to development and management of health; Government policies and interventions · GS3 › Issues relating to intellectual property rights · GS4 › Ethics in business
summary: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP; the editorial argues the cap alone will not make treatment affordable.
ideas: The cap tackles only the middlemen: it limits the margin on sale to patients, not the price at which companies sell to distributors or hospitals. If that starting price is high, the drug stays unaffordable.
GS2 · Health / regulation
Capping trade margins treats the symptom downstream while the real cost is set upstream by the manufacturer's price.
Patents give pricing power: patented cancer drugs face little generic competition, so manufacturers control prices, and earlier caps on the same drugs did not stop prices from rising.
GS3 · IPR and access to medicines
Where patents shut out generics, price caps on margins cannot discipline the manufacturer's price.
Hidden discounts hide the real price: steep discounts on a few units to select corporate hospitals, with most stock sold higher, make the true market price hard for regulators to know.
GS2 · Regulatory capacity
Selective discounts distort the market price, so margin regulation needs scrutiny of manufacturers' prices and transparent sales data.
A blanket cap can backfire: pharmacies have genuine storage and handling costs; a rigid cap could disrupt supplies to underserved areas, and hospitals may pass costs on through higher room rents.
GS2 · Policy design
A blanket price cap risks shortages in underserved areas and cost-shifting by hospitals.
Price control works only with the health system: stronger public health services, wider insurance coverage and more research on generics must accompany the cap.
GS2 · Universal health coverage
Affordable cancer care needs price regulation backed by public health services, insurance and generics.
keywords: NPPA's tool of capping margins between manufacturer and patient
Trade Margin Rationalisation caps the chain's margin but leaves the manufacturer's price untouched.
Where the cost is set versus where the cap bites
Regulation that targets downstream margins misses upstream pricing power.
When the true market price cannot be known
Selective discounts create price opacity that defeats margin regulation.
Recovering a capped margin through other charges
Hospitals may offset drug caps by cost-shifting to room rents.
Health spending that pushes households into distress
Unaffordable cancer drugs are a leading cause of catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure.
Balancing affordable medicines with incentives for research
Drug pricing policy must balance access with incentives for innovation.
data: Average profit mark-up added by intermediaries (stockists, distributors, hospital pharmacies, wholesalers) on cancer drugs
Intermediaries add an average mark-up of about 170% on cancer drug prices (NPPA).
New cap on the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs
The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP.
Reported monthly cost of the breast cancer drug ribociclib, despite profit restrictions in 2019
Ribociclib's monthly cost reportedly rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 profit caps.
examples: Ribociclib
A breast cancer drug whose price rose despite margin caps
GS3 · IPR / drug pricing
Ribociclib shows that margin caps fail when patents leave the manufacturer's price unchecked.
Patients skipping doses
Unaffordable drugs lead patients to delay treatment, skip doses or stop medication
GS4
GS2 social justice · GS4 compassion
When cancer drugs are unaffordable, patients delay treatment or skip doses, turning cost into lost lives.
pyqs: The State's role against marketisation of healthcare: drug-price regulation is one such tool, with its limits.
Limits of the public health system and the private sector's role: affordable medicines are part of universal coverage.
Section 3(d) and the Novartis case: patents versus access to affordable medicines.

trend.t: Health questions moved from goals and access (MDGs 2013, universal coverage 2015, community-level care 2018) to the State's moral and practical role (primary health 2021) and, most recently, to containing the marketisation of healthcare (2024). In GS3, patents and access to medicines appeared in 2013.
trend.watch: The balance between the State and the private sector in health has come in 2015 and 2024. Regulation of the health market is a must-study area.
focus: State regulation of drug prices and hospital charges
Universal health coverage and out-of-pocket expenditure
Patents, generics and access to medicines
Public health infrastructure and insurance

potential: "Regulating trade margins alone cannot ensure affordable access to essential medicines in India." Critically examine. (15 marks)
Discuss the role of intellectual property rights in the pricing of life-saving drugs in India. How can access be balanced with innovation? (10 marks)
Examine the challenges in regulating the prices of medicines in India and suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Examine the challenges in regulating the prices of medicines in India and suggest measures.
parts: Introduction: the price cap in one line, with facts

answer.t: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP, where intermediaries added an average 170% mark-up (NPPA).

pts.t: Margin caps do not cover the manufacturer's price to distributors and hospitals.
pts.ex: Ribociclib's cost rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 caps.

pts.t: Patented drugs face little generic competition, so prices stay high.
Selective discounts to corporate hospitals hide the real market price.
Hospitals may recover capped margins through room rents and other charges.
Rigid caps may make supply to underserved areas unviable for pharmacies.
Low insurance coverage leaves patients paying out of pocket.
pts.ex: Patients delay treatment or skip doses.

pts.t: Mandatory reporting of sales and discounts.
More research on and production of generic versions.
Strengthen public hospitals and coverage for cancer care.
Allow for legitimate storage and handling costs.

answer.t: Price caps can lower bills, but only a strong public health system can make cancer care truly affordable.

title: May make banks pay digital arrest victims if no due diligence: SC
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Ananthakrishnan G)
syllabus: GS3 › Challenges to internal security through communication networks; Basics of cyber security; Money laundering · GS2 › Structure and functioning of the judiciary; Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies · GS4 › Compassion towards the weaker sections; Probity
summary: In its own case on digital arrest scams, the Supreme Court said it may make banks compensate victims and face prosecution where poor due diligence enabled the fraud, and faulted the RBI for 'soft pedalling'.
ideas: A fraud on the economy: the Court called digital arrest the biggest financial fraud on the country's economy, running into thousands of crores; it is now a systemic threat, not a scattered crime.
GS3 · Cybercrime / financial security
Digital arrest scams, called by the Supreme Court the biggest financial fraud on the economy, have become a systemic cyber-security threat.

Accountability shifted to banks: the Court proposes that banks compensate victims and face prosecution if lapses enabled the fraud, with a mandatory rule to suspend unusual transactions until full verification.
GS3 banking · GS2 judiciary
Placing liability on banks that fail due diligence puts the cost of fraud on the institution best placed to stop it.
A regulator too soft: the Court faulted the RBI for consulting banks while the Court sought action against them, and called 'guidelines' too weak a word; rules need teeth.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Advisory guidelines invite regulatory soft-pedalling; mandatory rules with liability make regulators effective.
Insiders in the fraud: the Court noted that some bank officials are involved; the Attorney General said not every employee colludes and some have acted to stop frauds.
GS3 · Insider threat in banking
Insider collusion turns banks from the first line of defence into a channel for cyber fraud.

A three-level response: the Attorney General said prevention works through awareness, bank checks at the right stage, and RBI and MeitY rules due by December, and that complaints have fallen since the Court stepped in.
GS3 · Way forward
Countering digital arrest needs awareness, bank-level checks and binding regulation working together.
keywords: Scammers posing as officials hold victims in a fake 'arrest' over video calls until they pay
Digital arrest scams exploit fear of authority rather than technical loopholes.
Manipulating people psychologically rather than hacking systems
Digital arrest is social engineering: the weakest link is human fear, not software.
Making the party that can most easily prevent a loss bear it
Liability should rest with the actor best placed to stop fraud: the bank.
A regulator going easy on those it regulates
The Court's rebuke of the RBI warns against regulatory soft-pedalling.
Insider collusion makes internal controls as important as cyber defences.
A court acting on its own, without a petition
Through suo motu action, the Court made a scattered crime a matter of national accountability.
examples: The Supreme Court's suo motu case
The Court took up digital arrest scams on its own, without waiting for a petition
GS2 · Judiciary / people-centric governance
The Supreme Court's suo motu case on digital arrests shows the judiciary stepping in to protect citizens where others were slow.
Victim's money stays untouched, the bank pays
The proposed rule puts the burden on the strong institution, not the frightened individual
GS4
GS4 · Compassion towards the weaker sections
Making banks, not frightened victims, bear the loss reflects compassion towards the vulnerable.
Bank officials helping fraudsters
The Court noted some bank officials are involved in digital arrest frauds
GS4
GS4 · Corruption and probity
Insider collusion by bank officials is corruption that betrays the public trust placed in institutions.
Mandatory checks, not soft guidelines
The Court pushed the RBI to make transaction checks compulsory rather than advisory
GS2 · Proactive governance in regulation
Regulators must act before harm spreads: binding rules, not advisory guidelines.
pyqs: Types of cybercrime and measures: digital arrest is the newest major type, with bank liability as a measure.
A comprehensive cyber security strategy: financial fraud shows gaps across banks, regulators and citizens.
The growth of PIL and a powerful Supreme Court: suo motu action on digital arrest is a fresh example.
Independent, effective regulators: the Court's rebuke of the RBI's soft-pedalling.

trend.t: Cyber questions have come almost every year: cyber warfare (2013), the cyber security policy (2015), threats and frameworks (2017), data security (2018), CyberDome (2019), types of cybercrime (2020), cross-border attacks (2021) and a national strategy (2022). The focus has moved from threats to the state towards crimes against citizens and the institutional response.
trend.watch: Cyber security appeared every year from 2017 to 2022. It is a must-study GS3 area, now with financial fraud at its centre.
focus: Types of cybercrime, especially financial fraud
Institutional liability of banks and regulators
National cyber security strategy and coordination
Citizen awareness and digital literacy

potential: "Digital arrest scams expose gaps in both banking safeguards and regulatory enforcement." Discuss, and suggest a framework to protect citizens. (15 marks)
Should banks be held liable for losses suffered by victims of cyber fraud? Critically examine. (10 marks)
Examine the role of the Supreme Court's suo motu interventions in addressing gaps in governance, with recent examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: Should banks be held liable for losses suffered by victims of cyber fraud? Critically examine.
parts: Introduction: the Supreme Court's proposal in one line

answer.t: In October 2026 the Supreme Court proposed making banks compensate digital arrest victims where failure of due diligence enabled the fraud.

pts.t: Banks see transactions in real time and can stop unusual transfers.
Some frauds involve bank officials; liability strengthens internal controls.
Victims act under fear and manipulation; the system must protect them.
Liability pushes banks to invest in fraud detection.
Customers may become careless if banks always pay.
Compensation costs may be passed on to all customers.
Excessive holds may delay legitimate transactions.
Link liability to proven lapses in due diligence.
Mandatory RBI rules rather than advisory guidelines.
Citizen awareness that no agency 'arrests' anyone over a video call.

answer.t: Liability tied to due diligence can make banks the first line of defence against cyber fraud rather than its conduit.

title: Inter-State Council is a meeting point that has withered away. It must be rebuilt
syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; Issues and challenges pertaining to the federal structure; Centre-State relations; Constitutional bodies
summary: Shashi Tharoor argues that decisions like delimitation need the states' voice, and the Inter-State Council under Article 263, dormant for years, must be revived as an autonomous forum for Centre-state consultation.
evolution: Article 263 empowers the President to set up a council for Centre-state coordination.
Sarkaria Commission calls the dormant Inter-State Council the 'missing link'; the Council is constituted in 1990.
Long gaps between meetings; the Council works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Debate over a delimitation bill; Tharoor calls for reviving the Council before such decisions.
ideas: States must be heard on delimitation: deciding it in Parliament alone bypasses the states, an essential part of the federal system.
GS2 · Federalism / delimitation
A change as basic as delimitation should follow a national conversation that includes the states, not Parliament alone.
Article 263 envisioned a meeting point: the founders created the Inter-State Council to balance a strongly centralised Constitution in a diverse country.
GS2 · Constitutional bodies
Article 263 was meant to temper India's centralising Constitution with a forum for Centre-state coordination.
The 'missing link': the Council lay dormant for four decades and was set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice.
GS2 · Centre-state relations
The Sarkaria Commission called the dormant Inter-State Council the missing link in India's federal equilibrium.
Withered by design: without operational autonomy or regular meetings, it became an appendage of the Home Ministry, preferring unilateral policymaking over dialogue.
GS2 · Institutional weakness
Without operational autonomy or regular meetings, the Inter-State Council has become a minor arm of the Home Ministry.
Its atrophy erodes trust, especially with opposition-ruled states, as policy on tax, health, environment and security cuts across jurisdictions.
GS2 · Cooperative vs confrontational federalism
When the Inter-State Council is dormant, top-down policy breeds friction, especially with opposition-ruled states.
Rebuild it: an independent statutory secretariat, fixed meetings of the PM and CMs, and a role in major reforms, scheme reviews and inter-state disputes, giving 'cooperative federalism' a platform.
GS2 · Way forward
A revived Inter-State Council would give 'cooperative federalism' a platform, not just a slogan.
keywords: Constitutional basis for the Inter-State Council
Article 263 empowers the President to set up an Inter-State Council for Centre-state coordination.
Led to the Inter-State Council's creation in 1990
On the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation, the Inter-State Council was set up in 1990.
Freedom to set its agenda and function independently
The Council lacks the operational autonomy to act as a genuine federal forum.
Sarkaria's description of the dormant Inter-State Council
The Inter-State Council remains the missing link in India's federal equilibrium.
Centre and states working together as partners
Cooperative federalism has remained 'a platitude without a platform'.
Gradual weakening of an institution through neglect
Institutional atrophy has left a void at the heart of Indian federalism.
Redrawing seats and their distribution among states
Delimitation without the states' voice risks a federal crisis.
Mutual suspicion between the Centre and states
The Council's atrophy has deepened the Centre-state trust deficit.
examples: Inter-State Council (1990)
Set up on the Sarkaria Commission's advice, but met rarely and became a Home Ministry appendage
Weak federal institution
The Inter-State Council, set up in 1990, has met only at long intervals.
Delimitation debate (2026)
A bill feared to tilt seats towards some states, with no forum for states' views
Need for consultation
The 2026 delimitation debate shows why states need a formal forum.
pyqs: Directly usable: drawbacks of cooperative federalism; a dormant Inter-State Council is one.
Cooperation, competition, confrontation: a dormant Council tilts the balance to confrontation.
Recent changes in Centre-state relations; measures to build trust include reviving the Inter-State Council.
Dispute-resolution mechanisms in the federal framework: the Inter-State Council is the constitutional one.
Regional parties seek autonomy; a forum for states' views eases the tension.
Federalism as a basic feature is weakened when states are not consulted.

trend.t: Federalism has been asked almost every year: cooperative federalism (2015), cooperation versus confrontation (2020), national versus regional parties (2022), recent changes in Centre-state relations (2024), fiscal relations (2025) and dispute-resolution mechanisms (2026), alongside the Governor (2022, 2026) and Article 356 (2023). The focus has moved from the nature of Indian federalism to the institutions that should make it work.
trend.watch: Centre-state relations come up in nearly every GS2 paper. Institutional mechanisms (Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, GST Council, Finance Commission) and delimitation are must-study.
focus: Reviving the Inter-State Council and other Centre-state forums
Delimitation and the balance between states
The Governor's role and Centre-state friction
Fiscal federalism: GST, Finance Commission, state finances

Should delimitation of constituencies be preceded by consultation with the states? Discuss in the context of Indian federalism. (10 marks)
'Cooperative federalism has remained a platitude without a platform.' Critically examine. (10 marks)

practice.q: The Inter-State Council has remained a 'missing link' in India's federal structure. Examine the reasons for its ineffectiveness and suggest measures to make it a genuine platform for cooperative federalism.
parts: Introduction: Article 263, Sarkaria, 1990 (one line, with facts)

answer.t: Envisaged under Article 263 and set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice, the Inter-State Council has met rarely, leaving Centre-state dialogue without a forum.

pts.t: A forum where states shape national policy in a diverse country.
Tax, health, environment and security cut across jurisdictions.
Delimitation and resource sharing need states' consent.
A neutral platform for Centre-state and inter-state disputes.
Regular dialogue reduces friction and litigation.
States can assess the local impact of central schemes.
It works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Years pass between meetings despite the obligation to meet.
Its recommendations do not bind the Centre.
Governments favour central decisions or informal deals.
Opposition-ruled states see it as a Centre-controlled forum.
NITI Aayog and other bodies dilute its role.
Convene the PM, key ministers and CMs at regular intervals.
A statutory secretariat with civil servants and experts.
Require consultation on delimitation, major reforms and state-specific laws.
Use it for inter-state disputes on water, resources and infrastructure.
A working model of shared decision-making.
No new law is needed; Article 263 already allows it.

answer.t: Reviving the Inter-State Council would give cooperative federalism a platform, turning Centre-state relations from confrontation into partnership.
